meta.title: Who really said "Everything in the world is about sex, except sex"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Oscar Wilde — no Wilde source exists and the saying is barely thirty years old. Earliest located instance: Michael Cunningham in Provincetown Arts, July 1995, who disclaimed writing it. The psychiatrist Robert Michels is the best rival candidate, but the only citation for him is 2002, seven years later.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Everything in the world is about sex, except sex'?
meta.ogDescription: Wilde died in 1900; the saying first surfaces in 1995, in a psychoanalytic register, and nobody who used it early on claimed to have coined it.

answer.label: Not Oscar Wilde — an anonymous saying from the 1990s
answer.authorDates: Earliest located instance July 1995 · author unidentified
answer.sourceLine: There is no Wilde source for this. It appears in none of his plays, essays, letters or recorded conversation, and it is absent from Ralph Keyes’s compendium of the genuine Wilde epigrams. The earliest instance anyone has located is from July 1995 — Michael Cunningham, speaking in an interview with Paul Lisicky in Provincetown Arts (vol. 11, p. 39), who used it and then said it was not his. The psychiatrist Robert Michels is the best rival candidate, but the only citation for him is 2002, seven years later.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Psychoanalytic — every early instance is clinical

source.excerpt: Everything in human life is really about sex, except sex. Sex is about power.
trail: July 1995 — the earliest instance located. Michael Cunningham, speaking in an interview with Paul Lisicky in the journal Provincetown Arts (vol. 11, p. 39), uses the sentence and disclaims coining it, offering Wilde only tentatively (‘I think Oscar Wilde said…’). His phrasing implies he had already heard the line credited to Wilde; no earlier source for either the saying or the credit has been found, so who first attached Wilde’s name is not established the trail ↗.

1995 — the psychiatrist Robert Klitzman, in In a House of Dreams and Glass, gives a clinical variant he attributes to an unnamed supervisor: everything in therapy is really about sex except sex, which is about aggression. 1997 — Susan C. Vaughan repeats that form in The Talking Cure. The saying is clearly shop-floor psychoanalytic wisdom before it is a literary epigram.

2002 — the closest early match to the wording people now quote appears in a chapter by the psychoanalyst Robert Alan Glick, ‘Looking at women: what do men see?’, in Constructing and Deconstructing Woman’s Power (eds. Beth J. Seelig, Robert A. Paul and Carol B. Levy), where Robert Michels is quoted (as a personal communication) saying ‘everything is about sex, except sex: sex is about power’ — and immediately adding ‘sometimes sex is just about sex!’ Michels’s version is the earliest located instance close to the modern wording; he did not coin it, because the saying was already in print in 1995.

2013 — Frank Underwood says it in the first season of House of Cards, and the saying goes from clinical in-joke to universal caption. Quote Investigator’s verdict after all of this is that the saying remains anonymous.
source.excerptNote: The earliest located wording. Note what has since been sanded off: ‘in human life,’ and ‘really.’ And note what has been added: the wording most people search for — ‘everything in the world is about sex’ — matches no located source exactly; it is a later popular variant of the 1995 and 2002 forms. The 1995 form is a shrug about people; the version that circulates now sounds like a law.

source.rightsNote: We give no rights status, because there is no identified author to hang one on. The saying itself is an anonymous modern aphorism, first located in 1995 — too recent to be public domain by age, and with nobody to claim it. The individual texts in the trail (Cunningham 1995, Klitzman 1995, Vaughan 1997, Glick’s 2002 chapter, the House of Cards script) are each in copyright to their own authors, so quote the sentence, not their paragraphs. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Oscar Wilde
author.heading: Why it lands on Wilde
author.bio: Oscar Wilde died in Paris in 1900, ninety-five years before this sentence surfaces in print. He is the default owner of any epigram with a hinge in the middle — the trick of setting up a category and then exempting the one member of it you actually care about is genuinely his signature move, which is why the line passes the sniff test. It also helps that Wilde was tried and imprisoned over sex, so a hard-eyed remark about sex and power sounds like something he earned the right to say. He did not say it.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This one has an unusually clean disproof — the saying is younger than most of the people quoting it — and an unusually messy answer, because the real trail has several candidates and none of them claims it.

items.tag: no source, and 95 years too early
items.why: Nothing in the plays, essays, letters or reported conversation. Absent from Ralph Keyes’s The Wit & Wisdom of Oscar Wilde. Wilde died in 1900; the saying first appears in 1995. The credit seems to have started as a tentative guess by Michael Cunningham in that very first instance, and the guess hardened into a fact somewhere in the next decade the trail ↗.

The psychiatrist Robert Michels is quoted in a 2002 volume giving the wording everyone now uses. It is a genuine, citable attribution for that wording — but the saying was already in print in 1995, so he cannot be the originator. He is also the only person in the chain who added a punchline: ‘sometimes sex is just about sex.’

items.who: Michael Cunningham — used it, disclaimed it
items.why: The novelist’s words in a 1995 Provincetown Arts interview (with Paul Lisicky) are the earliest instance located, and he disclaimed them in the same breath — a spoken aside, not a written claim of authorship. Being first into print is not the same as being the author, and he is careful about the difference in a way that everyone downstream was not.

The 1995 Klitzman and 1997 Vaughan forms end with aggression, not power, and are set in the consulting room rather than the world. That is almost certainly the parent form: an anonymous joke passed between analysts, which someone later widened from therapy to everything.
The 2013 line in the show is where most people met it. Quoting a television villain is fine; quoting him as Oscar Wilde is not.

misattribution.truthLine: An anonymous saying out of psychoanalytic shop talk, in print by 1995, with the closest early match to the modern wording a 2002 remark by Robert Michels (reported as a personal communication), and made famous by House of Cards in 2013. Oscar Wilde has no connection to it at all the trail ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It is a demolition of Freud that keeps Freud’s shape. The joke only works if you already believe the everything-is-sex line, and it lands because it takes that idea seriously enough to follow it one step further and out the other side.

It is also an excellent thing to say and a poor thing to think about. Once you accept it, every human transaction becomes a power reading, which is exactly the sort of totalising explanation the sentence is mocking. Michels seems to have known this, which is why he added the second half nobody quotes: sometimes sex is just about sex.
detailsBody: July 1995: Michael Cunningham, in an interview with Paul Lisicky in Provincetown Arts (vol. 11, p. 39) — earliest located instance, and he disclaims it.
1995: Robert Klitzman, In a House of Dreams and Glass — clinical variant, ending in aggression, credited to an unnamed supervisor.
1997: Susan C. Vaughan, The Talking Cure — the same clinical variant.

2002: Robert Michels (personal communication), quoted in Robert Alan Glick’s chapter in Constructing and Deconstructing Woman’s Power (eds. Beth J. Seelig, Robert A. Paul and Carol B. Levy) — the closest early match to the modern wording, plus ‘sometimes sex is just about sex.’
2013: Frank Underwood, House of Cards — the line goes global. The show credits nobody; the Wilde ascription was already circulating independently.
context.pull: The man usually named as the author said it in 2002. The saying was already in print in 1995.
